title: Glory, food and clothing in the law and the Gospel
source_text: Πάλιν τε αὖ τὸ δόξης ἀντιποιεῖσθαι τῆς παρ᾿ ἀνθρώποις οὐ κατὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ μόνου διδασκαλίαν κωλύεσθαί φαμεν ἀλλὰ καὶ κατὰ τὴν παλαιὰν γραφήν. ἐπαρώμενος γοῦν ἑαυτῷ τις τῶν προφητῶν, εἰ ἔνοχος εἴη τοῖς ἁμαρτήμασι, φησὶν ἀντὶ μεγίστου κακοῦ συμβῆναι ἂν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν βιωτικὴν δόξαν. λέγει δὲ οὕτως· „κύριε, ὁ θεός μου, εἰ ἐποίησα τοῦτο, εἰ ἔστιν ἀδικία ἐν χερσί μου, εἰ ἀνταπέδωκα τοῖς ἀνταποδιδοῦσί μοι κακὰ, ἀποπέσοιμι ἄρα ἀπὸ τῶν ἐχθρῶν μου κενός· καταδιώξαι ἄρα ὁ ἐχθρὸς τὴν ψυχήν μου καὶ καταλάβοι, καὶ καταπατήσαι εἰς γῆν τὴν ζωήν μου, καὶ τὴν δόξαν μου εἰς χοῦν κατασκηνώσαι.“ ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τὸ „μὴ μεριμνᾶτε τί φάγητε ἢ τί πίητε. κατανοήσατε τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ἢ κατανοήσατε τοὺς κόρακας, ὅτι οὐ σπείρουσιν οὐδὲ θερίζουσι, καὶ ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν ὁ οὐράνιος τρέφει αὐτά, πόσῳ μᾶλλον ὑμεῖς διαφέρετε τῶν πετεινῶν;“ καὶ „περὶ ἐνδύματος τί μεριμνᾶτε; καταμάθετε τὰ κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς ἐναντία ἐστὶ ταῖς ἐν τῷ νόμῳ εὐλογίαις. διδασκούσαις τὸν δίκαιον ἐσθίοντα πληροῦσθαι, καὶ τῷ ὑπὸ τοῦ Σολομῶντος τοῦτον εἰρημένῳ τὸν τρόπον· „δίκαιος ἐσθίων ἐμπίπλησι ψυχὴν, ψυχαὶ δὲ ἀσεβῶν ἐνδεεῖς.“ χρὴ γὰρ ὁρᾶν τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς τροφὴν δηλουμένην ἐν τῇ κατὰ τὸν νόμον εὐλογίᾳ· ἧς οὐχ ὁ σύνθετος πληροῦται ἄνθρωπος ἀλλ᾿ ἡ ψυχὴ μόνη. ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου λαμβάνειν δεῖ τάχα μέν τι καὶ βαθύτερον τάχα δέ τι καὶ ἁπλούστερον, ὅτι χρὴ μὴ ξενίζεσθαι ταῖς περὶ τῶν τροφῶν καὶ ἐνδυμάτων τὴν ψυχὴν φροντίσιν, ἀλλ᾿ εὐτέλειαν ἀσκοῦντα πεπεῖσθαι ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ προνοεῖσθαι, εἰ μόνων τις τῶν ἀναγκαίων φροντίζοι.
pass_a_gloss: Again also we say that to lay claim to glory (δόξα) from men is forbidden (κωλύω) not according to the teaching (διδασκαλία) of Jesus alone but also according to the old writing. Cursing (ἐπαράομαι) himself, then, one of the prophets, if he should be liable (ἔνοχος) to the sins (ἁμαρτήματα), says that in place of (ἀντί) the greatest evil (κακόν) there would befall (συμβαίνω) him also worldly/life-bound (βιωτικός) glory. He says thus: 'Lord, my God, if I did this, if there is injustice (ἀδικία) in my hands, if I repaid (ἀνταποδίδωμι) to those repaying me evils, may I then fall away (ἀποπίπτω) from my enemies empty (κενός); may the enemy pursue (καταδιώκω) my soul (ψυχή) and overtake (καταλαμβάνω), and trample (καταπατέω) into earth my life (ζωή), and make my glory dwell (κατασκηνόω) in dust (χοῦς).' But neither is 'do not be anxious (μεριμνάω) what you eat or what you drink; consider (κατανοέω) the birds (πετεινά) of heaven, or consider the ravens (κόρακες), that they do not sow (σπείρω) nor reap (θερίζω), and our heavenly (οὐράνιος) Father feeds (τρέφω) them; how much more do you differ from the birds?' and 'about clothing (ἔνδυμα) why are you anxious? learn from (καταμανθάνω) the lilies (κρίνα) of the field' and the rest contrary (ἐναντίος) to the blessings (εὐλογίαι) in the law (νόμος) teaching that the righteous man eating is filled (πληρόω), and to what was said by Solomon in this way: 'a righteous man eating fills (ἐμπίπλημι) soul, but souls of the ungodly (ἀσεβεῖς) are in want (ἐνδεής).' For one must see (ὁράω) the food (τροφή) of the soul shown (δηλόω) in the blessing according to the law; with which not the composite (σύνθετος) man is filled but the soul alone. From the gospel (εὐαγγέλιον) one must take perhaps something deeper (βαθύτερον) and perhaps something simpler (ἁπλούστερον): that one must not be estranged/distracted (ξενίζω) in soul by the cares (φροντίδες) about foods and clothes, but practising (ἀσκέω) frugality (εὐτέλεια) be persuaded (πείθω, perf.) to be provided for by God, if one takes thought (φροντίζω) only for necessities (ἀναγκαῖα).
pass_b_english: Again, we say that laying claim to glory from men is forbidden not by the teaching of Jesus alone but also by the old Scripture. One of the prophets, at any rate, calling down a curse on himself if he should be guilty of those sins, says that worldly glory too would come upon him as the greatest of evils. He speaks thus: “O Lord my God, if I have done this, if there is injustice in my hands, if I have repaid with evil those who repaid me, then may I fall away empty before my enemies; may the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and trample my life into the ground, and make my glory dwell in the dust” (Psalm 7:3–5).

Nor, again, are these sayings contrary to the blessings in the Law, which teach that the righteous man eats and is filled (compare Leviticus 26:5; Deuteronomy 11:15): “Do not be anxious about what you will eat or what you will drink. Consider the birds of the air,” or, “Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, and our heavenly Father feeds them. How much more do you surpass the birds?” (Matthew 6:25–26; Luke 12:24), and “Why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field” (Matthew 6:28), and what follows. Nor are they contrary to what Solomon said in these words: “A righteous man eats and fills his soul, but the souls of the ungodly are in want” (Proverbs 13:25).

For we must see that the blessing in the Law makes known the food of the soul, with which it is not the composite man that is filled, but the soul alone. From the Gospel, however, we should perhaps take something deeper, and perhaps also something simpler: that one must not let the soul be distracted by cares about food and clothing, but, practising plain living, be confident of being provided for by God, if one takes thought only for what is necessary.

choices.choice: The prophet is David; the quotation is Septuagint Psalm 7:4–6, which is English Psalm 7:3–5 (LXX numbering converted). Origen reads the last clause, ‘make my glory dwell in the dust’, as worldly glory counted among the curses: ἀντὶ μεγίστου κακοῦ συμβῆναι ἂν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν βιωτικὴν δόξαν is rendered ‘worldly glory too would come upon him as the greatest of evils’. ἀποπέσοιμι ἄρα ἀπὸ τῶν ἐχθρῶν μου κενός follows the Septuagint (‘fall away empty before/from my enemies’). ‘Glory from men’ may echo John 5:41, 44 (δόξαν παρὰ ἀνθρώπων), but the wording is general, so it is not cited inline. The Gospel quotation blends Matthew 6:25–26 (birds of the air) and Luke 12:24 (ravens, πόσῳ μᾶλλον ὑμεῖς διαφέρετε τῶν πετεινῶν); the ‘or consider the ravens’ marks Origen’s own pairing of the two Gospels. Origen’s text reads ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν (‘our heavenly Father’); Matthew 6:26 has ὑμῶν (‘your’); translated as printed. Matthew 6:28 has καταμάθετε, as Origen does; compare Luke 12:27. The ‘blessings in the Law’ that promise eating and being filled are not quoted; Leviticus 26:5 (φάγεσθε τὸν ἄρτον ὑμῶν εἰς πλησμονήν) and Deuteronomy 11:15 (φάγῃ καὶ ἐμπλησθήσῃ) are given with ‘compare’ as representative passages (see also Leviticus 25:19; Deuteronomy 6:11). Proverbs 13:25 Septuagint: δίκαιος ἔσθων ἐμπιπλᾷ τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ. The sentence ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ τὸ ... ἐναντία ἐστί is reordered in English (the ‘blessings’ clause first) so that the long quotation does not separate subject and verb; nothing is omitted. ξενίζεσθαι ... τὴν ψυχήν literally ‘be estranged/disturbed in soul’; rendered ‘let the soul be distracted’. The copy-text’s full stop before διδασκούσαις is read as a comma.
